 13|
 14|# Rules - Conciseness
 15|
 16|The conciseness layer above the Human Voice card: what to cut, what is never cut, and the test that decides which is which.
 17|
 18|**Loading Condition:** ALWAYS, and rules only. A file paid for on every turn stays small enough to be worth paying for
 19|**Purpose:** Carries the cut rules, the keep rules and the reconstruction test that decides between them, so every delivery is sized as well as checked for banned wording
 20|**Scope:** Quantity, structure and load-bearing-ness, so an artifact that clears every hard blocker is not still three times too long. Nothing routes to it, since being ALWAYS-loaded is what makes it unroutable
 21|**Output Path:** None. The layer governs the length of an artifact another file writes, and produces none of its own
 22|**Loads With:** the consuming system's skill entry and `Rules - Human Voice Core`. That card governs word choice and this file governs quantity, so both run on every delivery
 23|**Authority:** `Rules - Conciseness - On Demand Rationale` carries the reason behind every rule below, the vocabulary candidates that were refused, the worked cut and keep pairs, and the roster of what blocks against what advises. Load it ON_DEMAND before changing a rule, never in order to write one. Both files share one numbering, so a section present in one and absent here lives there and keeps its number. That is why this card runs 5, 7, 8, 12 rather than counting straight, and why renumbering it would break the Section 8 citations three skills carry
 24|
 25|---
 26|
 27|## 1. THE TWO-SIDED CONTRACT
 28|
 29|Cuts and keeps here are edits rather than scored penalties, so they never count toward a system's hard blocker total. The two halves are load-bearing in equal measure: read only the cut half and the output arrives compressed until the reasoning falls out of it, and read only the keep half and nothing ever gets shorter. Every rule the validator blocks on arrives in a pair at the same strength, so the gate cannot be satisfied by cutting alone.
 30|
 31|---
 32|
 33|## 2. THE RECONSTRUCTION TEST
 34|
 35|After a cut, could a reader who does not already know the answer recover what was removed from what remains? If yes, the cut was free. If no, the information moved into the reader's head, which is loss wearing the shape of compression. Apply it per cut and never per document, because a document-level verdict is a judgement about length and length is the judgement that strips connectives. The reader it asks about is the one who opens the artifact three weeks later with no memory of the conversation that produced it.
 36|
 37|---
 38|
 39|## 3. CUT RULES
 40|
 41|### 3.1 The named rules
 42|
 43|- **Question echo.** An opening that restates the prompt before answering it
 44|- **Intent narration.** Announcing the move instead of making it
 45|- **Compliance acknowledgement.** Agreeing to do the work at the top of the work
 46|- **Terminal recap.** A closing paragraph that repeats the body, even accurately
 47|- **Hedge stack.** Two or more uncertainty markers on one claim. Keep the one that is true
 48|- **Importance assertion.** A sentence whose only content is that something matters
 49|- **The conclusion move.** The whole paragraph, not only the phrase that opens it
 50|- **Both-sides padding.** Symmetric pro and con on a question that is not symmetric
 51|- **Empty enumeration.** Naming that there are several things, listing them, analysing none
 52|- **Heading echo.** A first sentence that restates its own heading
 53|- **Restated constraint.** Repeating back a fact the user supplied
 54|- **Effort reporting.** Narrating the work done rather than what it found
 55|- **Count padding.** An item added so a list carries a different number of items. The triad rule counts triads per 150 words and bans none, so leave the count alone and cut something that was never load-bearing
 56|
 57|### 3.2 The stated vocabulary
 58|
 59|The validator blocks on exactly the terms below, so this list and the gate are one list, and adding a term to either alone is the drift that kept these checks advisory. Section 3.3 of the on-demand rationale records every candidate refused, with the correct writing each would have failed.
 60|
 61|Never open a sentence with: "In conclusion", "In summary", "To summarize", "To summarise", "To recap", "To sum up", "It's worth noting", "It is worth noting", "It's important to note", "It is important to note", "Let's explore", "Let's dive in", "Let's take a look", "At the end of the day", "Without further ado", "As we all know", "It goes without saying", "First and foremost", "Last but not least", "With that in mind", "On that note", "That said", "Needless to say", "Simply put", "In essence", "At its core", "In the world of", "When it comes to", "At a high level", "As you can see", "As mentioned above", "As noted above", "As previously noted", "As we have seen", "As discussed above", "In this section", "Put simply", "Generally speaking", "Broadly speaking", "The key takeaway", "The fact of the matter is", "It should be noted", "It must be noted", "By way of background".
 62|
 63|Never close a section on: "In summary", "In conclusion", "To summarize", "To summarise", "To recap", "To sum up", "In short", "All in all", "Overall", "Ultimately", "In closing", "To conclude", "To wrap up", "The takeaway", "Net net", "In a nutshell", "Long story short", "To put it simply", "On the whole".
 64|
 65|At most one hedge per claim: "might", "may", "could", "perhaps", "maybe", "possibly", "potentially", "probably", "seems", "appears", "arguably", "somewhat", "relatively", "presumably", "likely", "generally", "typically", "I think", "I believe", "tends to", "to some extent", "in some cases", "apparently", "conceivably", "ostensibly", "seemingly", "in theory", "I suspect", "My sense is".
 66|
 67|A cross-reference that names its target stays legitimate, so "As noted above" is banned while "the payout window defined under The weekly cycle" is not. A heading followed by a sentence that shares its words and adds no new one is a heading echo: cut the sentence and open on substance.
 68|
 69|### 3.4 The two cut rules the validator settles alone
 70|
 71|Both resolve without judgement, so the validator blocks on them in a deliverable and reports them as advice on an instruction file.
 72|
 73|**Importance assertion.** A sentence of twelve words or fewer carrying one of "important", "critical", "essential", "crucial", "vital", "matters", "significant", "noteworthy" or "fundamental", and carrying no content word of its own beyond that marker and generic filler. A sentence that names what matters and why is left alone.
 74|
 75|**Effort reporting.** A sentence opening on "I" or "We" that reaches one of "analysed", "analyzed", "reviewed", "checked", "scored", "scanned", "verified", "examined", "evaluated", "assessed", "investigated" or "audited" within the next few words. A quoted mention is left alone, and so is a sentence whose subject is the process the artifact documents rather than the author. State what the work found, since the work itself is not the deliverable.
 76|
 77|---
 78|
 79|## 4. KEEP RULES
 80|
 81|The anti-robotic half, at the same weight as the cut list. Each item names what a compression pass destroys first.
 82|
 83|- **Semantic connectives.** `because`, `so`, `which means`, `unless`, `otherwise`, `since` carry the logic, and deleting one turns an argument into a pile of assertions. The Human Voice cap on `however`, `furthermore`, `moreover`, `additionally` and `consequently` limits rhetoric and never reaches these
 84|- **One concrete instance per non-obvious rule.** The example is what makes a rule applicable
 85|- **The caveat that prevents a wrong action.** A reader who follows the trimmed version and breaks something was not served by the trim
 86|- **The scope qualifier.** `when`, `only when`, `for X but not Y`. A rule stripped of its scope is applied everywhere
 87|- **The noun behind a pronoun.** Name it again once the referent sits more than a clause away
 88|- **The negative case.** "A path string is not verification" is where the reader learns the boundary
 89|- **The specific number.** 33 fixtures, not several fixtures
 90|- **One human beat per roughly 400 words.** An aside, a judgement, a plain admission of what is unknown
 91|- **Grammar.** Articles, copulas and finite verbs are never a compression target, because conciseness removes claims and never syntax
 92|
 93|---
 94|
 95|## 5. OVER-COMPRESSION SIGNATURES
 96|
 97|### 5.1 The five shapes
 98|
 99|- **Connective stripping.** Clauses sit next to each other with the relation deleted, so the reader guesses whether the second causes, qualifies or contradicts the first
100|- **Referent stripping.** Pronouns and bare nouns left with their antecedents cut away
101|- **Telegraphese.** Dropped articles and copulas, verbless fragments, headline grammar in body text
102|- **Condition collapse.** A conditional rule flattened into an absolute one, which is a correctness bug rather than a style one
103|- **Example deletion.** An abstract rule left with nothing showing what it looks like in use
104|
105|### 5.2 The two the validator counts, and the perimeter they are measured over
106|
107|Connective stripping and telegraphese leave a numeric trace, so the validator counts them and blocks on a deliverable below either floor. Repair a document that trips one by naming the deleted relations back in and restoring the subject behind every stranded pronoun, never by adding words.
108|
109|- **Connective floor.** At least 5 semantic connectives per 1000 words of prose
110|- **Article floor.** At least 30 articles per 1000 words of prose
111|
112|Both floors are measured over paragraph prose alone, because a ratio only means something where sentences carry the reasoning. Outside the perimeter: frontmatter, a heading at any level, a bullet, a numbered item, a table row, a blockquote, an image, a horizontal rule, a field line such as `**Placement:** Creator deals dashboard`, a hashtag or handle run, a label line whose whole content is one bold or underlined run such as `**Most authentic**`, anything inside a fenced code block, and any HTML comment. Below 200 words of paragraph prose neither floor is applied, since a ratio over fewer words than that is noise.
113|
114|---
115|
116|## 7. FORMAT
117|
118|Prose, bullets and tables are not interchangeable, and picking wrong is how a short answer still reads badly. Three questions decide and the first yes wins: prose where the items differ in weight or their order encodes reasoning, a table where every row shares the same fields, bullets where the items are parallel, independently actionable and three to seven in number. Anything reaching the end without a yes is one paragraph pretending to be a list. Over-bulleting is the main way output turns robotic while looking concise, and the tells are verbless fragments, a bullet that needs the one above it to parse, and a list whose connectives were deleted so the items would line up. Heading density scales with length: under 300 words no headings, above that one per 150 to 400 words.
119|
120|---
121|
122|## 8. WHAT A DELIVERABLE NEVER CONTAINS
123|
124|The reasoning that produced an artifact, the score it earned and the assumptions it rests on are real work, and they belong in the reply beside the export path rather than inside the file the reader opens.
125|
126|### 8.1 The enumeration
127|
128|- A scoring section of any kind, whether headed MEQT, HVR, DEAL scoring, Scoring, Self-scan, Hard blockers or Weakest
129|- A dimension breakdown line, such as `M 4 · E 6 · Q 6 · T 3 · D 3` or its `D · E · A · L` equivalent
130|- A total, a floor status, a pass or fail verdict, or a score band action
131|- A hard blocker count or a voice self-scan line, in any wording
132|- Score commentary, such as a line opening `Weakest:` and naming which dimensions were thin
133|- An improvement-cycle note, an iteration count or a re-score history
134|- A bracketed `[Assumes: ...]` tag
135|- A methodology transcript, a perspective roster, an energy level or a phase-flow trace
136|- A validation checklist, a gate roster or a template-compliance report
137|- An attestation footer, a Mode header in visible text, a Template version in visible text, or any other processing metadata
138|
139|### 8.2 The one sanctioned exception
140|
141|Line 1 may carry a single HTML comment header, which renders as nothing and is the designed home for the mode, the framework, the score and the template version. A `Stats:` or `Assumes:` line written as an HTML comment directly below sits inside the same exception, for the same reason. Invisible when rendered is the whole test, so a score written as visible text is a violation wherever it sits in the file and a score written as a comment is fine wherever it sits.
142|
143|### 8.3 Where the reporting goes instead
144|
145|The reply carries what the artifact does not: the export path with read-back confirmation where the runtime can write files, the score and its verdict at the depth the mode calls for, the voice self-scan line naming the terms fixed and the terms kept with their reason, the assumptions in a form the user can correct before they harden, a short summary and one next step. Producing that report is the point, and moving it out of the artifact does not make it optional.
146|
147|### 8.4 Two narrow overrides
148|
149|Where the artifact refines a supplied source, never inject a Mode, Template, Perspectives, Quality Score or Energy header into preserved source structure, since the comment header is for a new artifact and a refinement keeps the source's own opening. Where the packaging renders the deliverable in a panel instead of saving a file, that rendered block is the artifact and the enumeration applies to it unchanged, the report follows the block, and the path is reported as export-equivalent rather than claimed as a save.
150|
151|---
152|
153|## 12. THE PRE-EXPORT PASS
154|
155|Run this after the voice pass and before the export, in order. The first two steps are the cut side and the last three are the keep side, and running only the cut side is the failure this layer exists to prevent.
156|
157|1. Delete every opener, recap and hedge stack named in Section 3.2, both shapes named in Section 3.4, and the question echo, intent narration, compliance acknowledgement and closing recap the body already carries, including the sentences after the phrase that opened one
158|2. Apply the reconstruction test to every remaining cut you are tempted to make, and stop at the first one that fails
159|3. Name every relation a reader would otherwise guess, then repair referent stripping, telegraphese and condition collapse in place
160|4. Confirm one concrete instance survives per non-obvious rule, one caveat survives per action that could go wrong, and the format matches the content under Section 7
161|5. Confirm the body carries nothing from Section 8.1, and that everything removed at this step now sits in the reply. This step is skipped most often, because the process material was correct work and deleting correct work feels wrong. It is not deleted, it moves
</file-view>

 33|Admin permissions follow the job. A CS agent can refund up to €200 per order, and a CS lead approves anything above that. Only merchandisers can create or change a promotion. Warehouse operators see orders and shipments but no payment details.
 34|
 35|A signed-in customer has an account with saved addresses and order history. A guest gives an email address at checkout and gets the order emails, but has no order history to come back to.
 36|
 37|## Glossary
 38|
 39|| Term | Meaning |
 40||------|---------|
 41|| Market | One of NL, BE, DE, FR or UK. Sets currency, VAT, shipping fees and the banner copy |
 42|| Unit | One item in the cart. A line with quantity 3 is 3 units |
 43|| Subtotal | The sum of the lines after promotions and before shipping |
 44|| Automatic promotion | A discount that applies without a code, set up by a merchandiser in Admin |
 45|| Discount code | A code the customer types in the cart or at checkout |
 46|| Sale item | A product whose `compare_at` price is higher than its price, shown struck through |
 47|| Dispatch cut-off | `15:00` Amsterdam time on a working day. Orders paid before it leave the warehouse the same day |
 48|| Collection | The parcel carrier's daily pickup at the warehouse, 18:00 on working days |
 49|| Parcel item | An item within the parcel carrier's limits of `30 kg` and `120 cm` on the longest side |
 50|| Pallet item | An item over either limit. It ships by the pallet carrier, which books a delivery slot with the customer by phone |
 51|| Label | The parcel carrier's shipping label for one parcel. Every label the carrier creates is charged |
 52|| WISMO | Where is my order, the helpdesk tag for order status contacts |
 53|| Return window | `30 days` from delivery |
 54|
 55|## Services and integrations
 56|
 57|Internal services are owned by the team named in the table. Each service has its own database and talks to the others over HTTP and the event queue.
 58|
 59|| Service | Owner | Does |
 60||---------|-------|------|
 61|| `cart-service` | Checkout | Carts for guests and signed-in customers, the badge count, line prices after automatic promotions |
 62|| `checkout-service` | Checkout | Address, shipping method, the payment session and order creation |
 63|| `promotions-service` | Merchandising tools | Automatic promotions, discount codes and the free-shipping threshold |
 64|| `orders-service` | Post-purchase | Orders, order status, refunds and the returns CS agents create |
 65|| `shipping-service` | Fulfilment | The parcel and pallet split, parcel labels and tracking numbers |
 66|| `accounts-service` | Storefront | Sign-in, addresses and the web wishlist |
 67|| `catalog-service` | Merchandising tools | Products, prices, `compare_at` prices and stock synced from the warehouse system |
 68|
 69|Third parties appear by role only:
 70|
 71|- Payments go through the payment provider: cards, wallet payments and local bank payment methods, through hosted fields on web and its SDK in the apps
 72|- Stock, picking and packing run in the warehouse system. orders-service sends it each paid order, and it reports back when the order is packed
 73|- Every parcel in all five markets goes with the parcel carrier. shipping-service creates labels through its API and receives label events by webhook
 74|- Pallet items go with the pallet carrier. shipping-service sends it a booking file once a day at 16:00, and it sends back no tracking events
 75|- Order, shipping and refund emails go out through the email delivery provider
 76|- Every CS contact sits in the helpdesk, tagged by topic
 77|
 78|## Teams and discipline codes
 79|
 80|Six teams build the product: Storefront (web and app shopping flows), Checkout, Post-purchase (orders, tracking and returns), Fulfilment (shipping-service and the carrier and warehouse integrations), Merchandising tools (Admin catalog and promotions) and Data. A small design system group sits with Storefront.
 81|
 82|Every task and bug carries one discipline code.
 83|
 84|| Code | Discipline |
 85||------|------------|
 86|| `FE` | Front end: web, iOS or Android client work |
 87|| `BE` | Back end: a service, a job or an integration |
 88|| `BO` | Back office: Admin screens and tools |
 89|| `FS` | Full stack: one change across client and service, or a parent task over platform subtasks |
 90|| `DATA` | Tracking plans, events and dashboards |
 91|| `DS` | Design system components and tokens |
 92|
 93|Task and bug titles follow `{Discipline} - {Surface} - {Feature code} - {Title}`, where the surface is `Web`, `iOS`, `Android` or `Admin`. Back-end and data work that no single surface owns drops the surface segment. Examples: `FE - Android - CHK - Postcode field rejects spaces`, `BO - Admin - RET - Return reason picker` and `BE - SHIP - Pallet booking file retries`.
 94|
 95|Story and epic titles carry no discipline code. A story is `{Persona or platform} - {Area or initiative} - {Feature}` and an epic is `Epic - {Persona or platform} - {Area or initiative}`, for example `Customer - Account - Address book` and `Epic - Customer - Delivery slots`.
 96|
 97|## Feature codes
 98|
 99|| Code | Area | Main service |
100||------|------|--------------|
101|| `CART` | Cart, mini cart and the cart badge | cart-service |
102|| `CHK` | Checkout: address, shipping method, payment, confirmation | checkout-service |
103|| `PROMO` | Automatic promotions, discount codes and the free-shipping banner | promotions-service |
104|| `SHIP` | Parcel and pallet split, labels, dispatch | shipping-service |
105|| `TRACK` | Order status and tracking after dispatch | orders-service, shipping-service |
106|| `RET` | Returns and refunds | orders-service |
107|| `ACCT` | Sign-in, account, addresses and order history | accounts-service |
108|| `WISH` | Wishlist on web and in the apps | accounts-service, app storage |
109|
110|A ticket takes the code of the area where the customer sees the change. Work that spans two areas takes the code of the area that owns the data.
111|
112|## Platforms and app versions
113|
114|| Platform | Current version | Released | Supported |
115||----------|-----------------|----------|-----------|
116|| iOS | `4.8.0` | 2026-09-08 | iOS 16 and later |
117|| Android | `4.8.2` | 2026-09-15 | Android 9 and later |
118|| Web | Deployed continuously | Several times a day | The two latest versions of each major browser |
119|
120|Both apps ship on a two-week cycle, on Tuesdays. Android went out as 4.8.0 on 2026-09-08 together with iOS, then took two hotfixes: 4.8.1 on 2026-09-10 for a checkout crash on some devices, and 4.8.2 on 2026-09-15 for push notification taps that opened the home screen. iOS has had no hotfix since 4.8.0. The next app release is 4.9.0.
121|
122|Within two weeks of a release about 80% of app sessions run the current version. Versions below 4.2 are forced to update. Web events carry the web build number in the same version field the apps use.
123|
124|## Currencies and locales
125|
126|| Market | Currency | Locales | Standard shipping | Free shipping threshold |
127||--------|----------|---------|-------------------|-------------------------|
128|| Netherlands | `EUR` | `nl-NL` | `€4.95` | €50 |
129|| Belgium | EUR | `nl-BE`, `fr-BE` | €4.95 | €50 |
130|| Germany | EUR | `de-DE` | €4.95 | €50 |
131|| France | EUR | `fr-FR` | €4.95 | €50 |
132|| United Kingdom | `GBP` | `en-GB` | `£3.95` | £45 |
133|
134|Prices include VAT at the market's rate. The storefront formats amounts for the locale, while tickets and internal documents write them in en-GB notation, as this table does. Every market also offers English through the language switcher, which shows en-GB copy with the market's own currency. Belgian customers pick Dutch or French on their first visit.
135|
136|UK parcels cross a customs border. The parcel carrier clears them on its cross-border service with duties paid by Fernhouse, and they take one to two working days longer than parcels inside the EU.
137|
138|## Key flows
139|
140|1. **Browse and add to cart.** A customer adds items from a product page or a product card, and the badge updates at once. Carts of signed-in customers follow them across web and the apps. Guest carts stay on the device for 14 days.
141|2. **Checkout.** Guest or signed in. The customer gives an address, gets standard shipping (plus a pallet delivery note when a pallet item is in the cart), then pays through the payment provider. Card details are typed in full on every order today, signed in or not. The order exists once the payment is authorised.
142|3. **Promotions.** Automatic promotions show on product pages and in the cart. A discount code goes in the cart or at checkout. How they combine is set out in the Promotions rules note that Merchandising owns.
143|4. **Fulfilment.** orders-service sends each paid order to the warehouse system. When picking starts, shipping-service asks the parcel carrier for one label per parcel, and the label arrives by webhook, usually within a minute. Orders paid before the `15:00` cut-off on a working day leave with the 18:00 collection.
144|5. **After dispatch.** The customer gets a shipping email with the tracking number. The order page on web and in the apps shows `Order placed` until dispatch and `Shipped` after it, with the tracking number, and it never changes after that. Customers who want more go to the parcel carrier's own tracking page.
145|6. **Returns.** Customers have `30 days` from delivery. There is no self-serve return today. The customer contacts CS, a CS agent creates the return in Admin and emails a return label, the warehouse checks the item, and the agent refunds. CS handles about `1,900` return requests a month, and a refund takes `6 days` on average from the first contact.
146|7. **Wishlist.** A heart on product cards and product pages. On web the wishlist is saved to the account and needs sign-in. In the apps it is saved on the device and works without an account. Both hold up to 50 items.
147|
148|## Known constraints
149|
150|- The parcel carrier takes parcels up to `30 kg` and `120 cm` on the longest side. Anything over either limit goes by the pallet carrier, which has no API and no tracking events
151|- The parcel carrier's API allows 20 requests per second for the whole account, shared by every call shipping-service makes
152|- Every label is charged when the carrier creates it, whether or not the parcel ships
153|- Card data stays with the payment provider. Fernhouse may store a card token, the last four digits and the expiry date, and nothing else
154|- App changes reach most customers about a week after release, because of store approval and slow updates. A fix that must land the same day has to be server-side
155|- Admin runs on desktop web only and is not built for phones
156|- Working days are Monday to Friday minus Dutch public holidays, because the warehouse is in the Netherlands
157|- Discounts are worked out in promotions-service only. Clients show what it returns and never compute a discount themselves
158|
159|## Analytics conventions
160|
161|- Event names follow `object_action` in snake_case, with the verb in the past tense: `product_viewed`, `cart_item_added`, `checkout_started`, `order_placed`, `wishlist_item_added`
162|- Every event carries `platform` (`web`, `ios` or `android`), `app_version`, `market` (`nl`, `be`, `de`, `fr` or `uk`), `locale` and `customer_type` (`guest` or `account`)
163|- Money goes in minor units with the currency beside it, as `value_cents` and `currency`
164|- A new event needs a row in the Data team's tracking plan and a DATA task before any FE task sends it
165|- Reporting reads from the analytics tool, never from raw event tables
</file-view>

 12|---
 13|
 14|# Product Owner Flow Templates
 15|
 16|Copy/apply patterns for Product Owner Flow Mode models.
 17|
 18|**Loading Condition:** CONDITIONAL, with `references/flow-mode.md` whenever Flow intent is selected
 19|**Purpose:** Provides the user-flow patterns, the provenance table every diagram type keeps and the reply shape every type delivers
 20|**Scope:** Five user-flow patterns, the intake questions, the provenance table and the reply shape. The other types keep their patterns in `assets/templates/`
 21|**Output Path:** None. The model is working data and the board is the deliverable
 22|
 23|---
 24|
 25|## 1. OVERVIEW
 26|
 27|### Purpose
 28|
 29|Every pattern below passes `scripts/flow_check.py` as a user flow, and `scripts/compose_board.py` composes it into a board. Start from the pattern closest to the flow, rename the nodes after the real screens and triggers, add the board lines below and run the check before the write gate. A process, an architecture, a sequence, a state diagram, an ER diagram or a gantt chart starts from its own file in `assets/templates/`, and keeps the provenance table and the reply shape below.
 30|
 31|### Usage
 32|
 33|- Node ids are short, stable and camelCase, because the provenance table names them, the composer names every layer after them and the generated fallback mis-routes an underscore
 34|- A label names the screen or the action a person takes, in the words the product uses, in one to four words where those words allow
 35|- A label with a parenthesis, a colon or a slash goes in double quotes, such as `pick["Pick a plan (monthly)"]`
 36|- A decision label is a question, and each exit label is one of its answers
 37|- Every connector is a solid arrow `-->`
 38|- A user flow and a process each carry exactly one `style` line, which marks the first glance. A styled goal, failing end or decision keeps its kind and takes a pink outline, and a styled step is drawn light pink. `style done fill:#CDF4D3,stroke:#66D575` makes that end the goal and the light red pair makes an end a failure. Every pair comes from `references/style-guide.md`, and any other colour is refused or counts as a second accent
 39|- Write `flowchart LR` unless the chain is short, because a board reads wider than it reads tall
 40|
 41|### Board lines
 42|
 43|The board's own text rides on `%%` comment lines, which the check ignores and the composer reads. Each one is optional, and the generated fallback strips them all:
 44|
 45|```text
 46|%% title: Start a return
 47|%% subtitle: How a customer starts a return in the app, from the order list to a confirmed return
 48|%% source: Sources: five app screenshots and the returns doc. Left out: free pickup over 100 euros, a proposal.
 49|%% zone: Find the order: orders, detail
 50|%% zone: Request the return: window, reason, method
 51|```
 52|
 53|- `%% title:` names the board. With none, the composer takes a Mermaid frontmatter title, a sequence or gantt `title` line, then `Diagram <n>`
 54|- `%% subtitle:` is one sentence under the title on who reads the board and why
 55|- `%% source:` is the line under the key naming the sources and what was left out
 56|- `%% zone: <label>: <id>, <id>` groups nodes in a tinted section. A user flow or a process without lanes reads its zones in flow order, and once a flow has zones every node sits in exactly one. An ER diagram draws each zone around its entities. Lanes and composite states are zones already, so a laned process, an architecture or a state diagram takes no zone line
 57|
 58|---
 59|
 60|## 2. PATTERNS
 61|
 62|### Linear flow
 63|
 64|```mermaid
 65|flowchart TD
 66|    start([Open the page]) --> step1[Fill in the form]
 67|    step1 --> step2[Submit]
 68|    step2 --> done([Confirmation shown])
 69|    style done fill:#CDF4D3,stroke:#66D575
 70|```
 71|
 72|### One decision
 73|
 74|```mermaid
 75|flowchart TD
 76|    start([Open the page]) --> step1[Submit the form]
 77|    step1 --> valid{Valid?}
 78|    valid -->|Yes| done([Confirmation shown])
 79|    valid -->|No| fix[Show the field errors]
 80|    fix --> step1
 81|    style done fill:#CDF4D3,stroke:#66D575
 82|```
 83|
 84|### Platform split with a merge dot
 85|
 86|```mermaid
 87|flowchart TD
 88|    start([Open the page]) --> open[Open the selector]
 89|    open --> device{Which device?}
 90|    device -->|Desktop| menu[Dropdown menu]
 91|    device -->|Mobile| sheet[Bottom sheet]
 92|    menu --> merge((.))
 93|    sheet --> merge
 94|    merge --> pick[Pick an item]
 95|    pick --> done([Item shown])
 96|    style done fill:#CDF4D3,stroke:#66D575
 97|```
 98|
 99|### Three outcomes
100|
101|```mermaid
102|flowchart TD
103|    start([Request sent]) --> result{Response?}
104|    result -->|Approved| done([Access granted])
105|    result -->|Rejected| reject([Reason shown])
106|    result -->|Needs info| ask[Ask for missing info]
107|    ask --> start
108|    style done fill:#CDF4D3,stroke:#66D575
109|```
110|
111|### A flow split across two diagrams
112|
113|Divide the ordered source list into groups of at most 9 nodes before the first Mermaid block, each group ending on a hand-off node that names it, so the split is read off the sources rather than a model that already overran. A flow over 9 nodes ends the first diagram on a named hand-off and starts the second diagram from the same name. Both diagrams go into the same file as two boards, read left to right: the second write passes the `fileKey` the first one used, and each board's `%% title:` carries its ordinal and its hand-off, such as `1. Sign up` and `2. Setup`. Every source step lands in one of the diagrams or is listed as left out under the provenance table.
114|
115|```mermaid
116|flowchart TD
117|    start([Sign up]) --> verify[Verify the email]
118|    verify --> profile[Fill in the profile]
119|    profile --> handoff([Continue to setup])
120|    style handoff fill:#CDF4D3,stroke:#66D575
121|```
122|
123|```mermaid
124|flowchart TD
125|    handoff([Continue to setup]) --> connect[Connect an account]
126|    connect --> done([Dashboard shown])
127|    style done fill:#CDF4D3,stroke:#66D575
128|```
129|
130|---
131|
132|## 3. PROVENANCE TABLE
133|
134|One row per item, written in the intake before any Mermaid, beside the model and never on the board. An item is a node, a state, a participant, an entity, a task or an edge. An edge earns a row whenever it was inferred rather than read off a source, because a row kept only for an edge whose ends differ leaves an inferred connector unclassified.
135|
136|| Item | Kind | Source | Source class | Confidence | Rung |
137||---|---|---|---|---|---|
138|| start | node | `<screenshot file, Figma node or doc section>` | current behavior | high | stated |
139|| valid | node | `<source that states the check>` | current behavior | high | stated |
140|| start to valid | edge | `<neighbouring frames with no stated move>` | current behavior | medium | `<ladder step>` |
141|
142|The source class is one of current behavior, approved direction, proposal, retired material and unknown. A row marked proposal or unknown carries its status into the node label, or the node is left out.
143|
144|The confidence is `high`, `medium` or `low`. `high` is an item a source states, `medium` is an item one source implies and `low` is an item the ladder reached by joining two sources. Confidence is not the Brief's status, which says whether a row was captured, so the two sit on one item without repeating each other. The rung is the step of the inference ladder in `references/flow-mode.md` Section 4 that produced the row, and it reads `stated` when a source states the item outright.
145|
146|A `medium` or `low` row carries its uncertainty in the node label or is left out, so the board never shows a confident shape over a thin source. A board has no marker to hide, so the label is where the uncertainty lives.
147|
148|Where a frame name and the frame's visible heading differ, both are recorded in the row and the heading labels the node, because the heading is what the reader sees. The difference is a finding for the playback and is never resolved in the row.
149|
150|Below the table, list every source item that is in no diagram, each with its reason. This is the fidelity ledger sk-design-diagram asks for, so a split or a cut at a lower detail level is named here too:
151|
152|```text
153|Left out: <source item>, <reason, such as retired material, a split that ends before it or a cut at the simplified detail level>
154|```
155|
156|---
157|
158|## 4. REPLY SHAPE
159|
160|```text
161|<board URL>
162|Read-back: <counts the type's reference names, each as n of n>
163|Extensions: <n> of <n> pins, <n> of <n> legend stickies, <n> overlaps
164|Left out: <source item>, <reason>
165|Finding: <a read-back finding, a write warning, an open item or a question>
166|HVR self-scan: <n> hard blockers. Fixed: <terms>. Kept with reason: <terms>.
167|```
168|
169|The `Read-back:` counts follow the type: nodes, connectors and labelled decision exits for a user flow, lanes as well for a process, participants and messages for a sequence, states and transitions for a state diagram, entities, relationships and attributes for an ER diagram, and sections, tasks and milestones for a gantt chart. The `Extensions:` line appears only when the write added any, and the `Left out:` line only when the provenance table lists items left out, so the user sees what the board does not hold. When only a screenshot could be read, the read-back line ends with `, read visually`, because a picture cannot prove which nodes a connector joins. When the connector has no read tool, the line is `Read-back: not possible, the connector has no read tool`, and the board is never called done.
170|
171|These lines are the whole reply, and the self-scan is always the last. Each finding, warning, open item or question is one `Finding:` line, and nothing follows the self-scan. The playback of the settled rows runs before the model and the gate, as `references/flow-mode.md` Section 8 sets out, and it never becomes a line here.
172|
173|---
174|
175|## 5. INTAKE QUESTIONS
176|
177|The type table in `references/flow-mode.md` Section 3 reads as questions. Ask them as an interview before the model is written, in three rounds that depend on each other, because an answer in one round settles what the next round may ask.
178|
179|| Round | Asks | Settles |
180||---|---|---|
181|| One | The reader, the question and the outcome | Who the board is for, what it must answer and what the reader decides next |
182|| Two | Entry, exit and actors | Where the flow starts, where it ends and who takes each step |
183|| Three | Decisions, states, sources and class | Where the flow branches, which states exist, which source states each fact and what class that source holds |
184|
185|### Every question carries a reading and a recommendation
186|
187|A user who does not know an answer should still be able to accept one, so every question is put in this shape:
188|
189|```text
190|Reading: <what the sources already show for this question>
191|Question: <the one thing still open>
192|Recommended: <the answer the AI would take>
193|Why: <the one line of reason>
194|```
195|
196|- One to three questions per round and no later round while an earlier one is open
197|- Never a question a supplied source already answers, because that answer is stated as the reading instead
198|- A round closes when each of its questions is answered, accepted or corrected
199|
200|### A vague answer is asked again
201|
202|An answer that names nothing is asked once more with one probe from this set, and never with the same wording twice:
203|
204|- A concrete scenario, such as one example walked from the first click to the end
205|- An edge case, such as two of these arriving at once
206|- A contradiction, such as one source stating this and another stating the opposite
207|- A term, such as what one word means in this product
208|- A scale, such as how many of these exist on a busy day
209|- A failure mode, such as what the reader sees when one step fails
210|- A boundary, such as where this flow stops and another one begins
211|
212|### An unanswered question is never a dead end
213|
214|When the user skips a question or says they do not know, the AI takes the recommended answer. That fact is marked assumed in the Brief and named in the playback before the gate, so the user corrects it before anything is written. A row the user corrects is recorded as `corrected` and counts as settled. No later round asks it again.
</file-view>

 12|---
 13|
 14|# FigJam Type - User Flow
 15|
 16|A user flow is the screens and choices one person passes through to reach a goal. It is the default Flow type and the strictest, because it is drawn from screenshots and frames a reader will compare node by node.
 17|
 18|**Loading Condition:** CONDITIONAL, when the Flow route draws a user flow
 19|**Purpose:** The grammar, rules, budget and read-back for a user flow
 20|**Pairs With:** `assets/flow-templates.md`
 21|
 22|---
 23|
 24|## 1. WHEN TO USE
 25|
 26|**The reader's question:** which screens does a person pass through, and where do they choose?
 27|
 28|- A flow drawn from screenshots, from Figma frames or from a product doc that walks one person through the product
 29|- A platform split, such as desktop and mobile, that rejoins on a later screen
 30|- A journey, which Flow Mode does not draw as such, redrawn as the screens it visits
 31|
 32|Use another type when several people or teams hand work to each other (a process), when the subject is services and stores (an architecture) or when time order between systems is the point (a sequence).
 33|
 34|---
 35|
 36|## 2. WHAT THE BOARD DRAWS
 37|
 38|`flowchart LR` or `flowchart TD`, composed into a board as Section 6 sets out. No `%% type:` line is needed, because a flowchart with none is a user flow.
 39|
 40|| Shape | Mermaid | Means |
 41||---|---|---|
 42|| Stadium | `id([Label])` | The flow starts or ends here |
 43|| Rectangle | `id[Label]` | A screen or an action |
 44|| Rhombus | `id{Label?}` | A choice, written as a question |
 45|| Circle | `id((.))` | A merge dot, where branches rejoin, with no words |
 46|
 47|Every connector is a solid one-way arrow, `-->`, with an optional label: `a -->|Yes| b`.
 48|
 49|On the board the first screen takes the `entry` role, every other screen the `neutral` role, a decision a diamond in the `decision` role, the goal the `goal` role and every other end the `exit` role, beside the main line rather than on it, and `assets/figjam-design.md` names the swatch each role draws.  64|- **Left to right or top to bottom,** the same way for every diagram of one flow. Left to right is the default, because the composer keeps the main route on one straight line across a board that reads wider than tall and sets each branch beside it. Top to bottom suits a short flow

191|## 5. TYPE AND GRID
192|
193|sk-design-diagram's type ramp and grid carry over, because the composer sets the font itself. Every board uses one family at one scale, Inter unless a design names another. A family FigJam cannot load falls back to Inter with a warning:
194|
195|| Text | Size | Weight |
196||---|---|---|
197|| Title | 64 | Bold |
198|| Subtitle | 28 | Regular, wrapped at the diagram's width between 960 and 1440 pixels and then narrowed while it keeps its number of lines, so its lines come out even |
199|| Zone and key names | 24 | Semi Bold |
200|| Node label | 20 | Medium |
201|| Edge label, key entry, source line | 18 | Medium on a connector, Regular elsewhere |
202|| Entity field | 16 | Regular |
203|| Gantt bar length, step pin | 14 | Medium |
204|
205|Every position and size sits on an 8 pixel grid. A shape grows from its kind's base size until its label fits inside it, with a 32 pixel inset in a round shape whose text FigJam clips to the inscribed box, and every shape of one kind on a board takes the size of the largest, so a rank reads as one row.
206|
207|The scale is tuned for a laptop at overview zoom. Reading distance does not change it, as `references/flow-mode.md` Section 4 sets out, and buys fewer nodes and shorter labels instead.
208|
209|A design re-maps meanings onto the pairs in Section 3 and never adds a colour. A board is shared and recoloured in FigJam, so a brand palette would turn every swatch into a custom colour. A brand colour asked for by name is a hand edit after the write, and the reply says it is off-palette.
210|
211|---
212|
213|## 6. WHAT HOLDS THE RECORD
214|
215|- `scripts/figjam_checks/common.py` holds the pairs the check accepts
216|- `assets/figjam-design.md` holds the design a board is drawn in, and `scripts/figjam_checks/design.py` reads it, checks every token against its floor and sends the composer only what differs from the built-in design
217|- `assets/compose-board.js` holds the built-in design, the swatches, the tints and the shapes, and `scripts/compose_board.py --self-test` measures the accent's hue, weight and ink on every board it composes and fails when the design file leaves out a token or breaks a floor
218|- `scripts/compose_board.py --design-check` prints the resolved design with its measured ratios and names every design warning
219|- The self-test fails when the record above names a pair the check does not accept, or the check accepts one the record does not name
220|- The self-test re-measures both ratio columns of every row and fails on any drift
221|
222|---
223|
224|## 7. SPACING
225|
226|Colour tells a reader what belongs together, but space tells them first. A reader groups what sits close before reading a label, so a board that spaces every gap the same reads as one flat field and its own structure disappears.
227|
228|| Band | Gap | What the gap separates |
229||---|---|---|
230|| One thought | 60 to 92 pixels | Two nodes a reader takes as one step or one idea |
231|| Same topic | 200 to 400 pixels | Two groups the board discusses one after the other |
232|| Another part of the board | 1000 pixels or more | Content that answers a different question |
233|
234|Two rules follow from the bands:
235|
236|- Two unrelated groups are never closer than the text blocks inside a card, so the gap between groups always reads wider than the gap within one
237|- A wrapper is larger than the group's own internal gap and smaller than the gap to the next group, so its edge never falls on a neighbour

  8|A board is slow to fix once it exists: the composer owns its layout, so every
  9|fix is a new write. Worse, neither the composer nor the generated fallback
 10|draws all that Mermaid can say, so a model can promise a reader something the
 11|board never shows. The rules each diagram kind carries are checked on the
 12|Mermaid model first, and a model that breaks one is never written. The same
 13|parse is measured, so a shape that is legal and still hard to read, such as a
 14|rank of six steps or a connector that doubles back, is caught here rather than
 15|on the board.
 16|
 17|Each Mermaid block in the file is one diagram, read by its header:
 18|
 19|- `flowchart` is a user flow unless a `%% type: process` or
 20|  `%% type: architecture` comment line says otherwise
 21|- `sequenceDiagram`, `stateDiagram-v2`, `erDiagram` and `gantt` are the other

 27|explains each one. Flowcharts and state diagrams are parsed by
 28|`vendored/mermaid_extract.py`, a byte copy of the shared diagram skill's
 29|extractor kept in step through `vendor.json`. It parses text only and never
 30|renders or runs anything in a label. Sequence, ER and gantt blocks are parsed
 31|by their own modules, because the extractor drops a sequence's dropped
 32|features, the fields of an aliased entity and every gantt chart. Every
